item.title: Aggregating treatment effects across multiple outcomes
item.description: arXiv:2611.05456v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Researchers often aggregate outcomes to estimate treatment effects on abstract concepts, such as "crime" or "wealth." First, I document that principal component analysis (PCA), inverse variance matrix (IVM) weighting, and standardized averaging (SA) are commonly used but have unexpected shortcomings. PCA can assign negative weights, need not maximize precision, depends on an arbitrary sign normalization, and can have nonstandard asymptotics. Unlike SA, IVM can assign negative weights, but neither necessarily maximizes precision. Second, I develop a statistical decision-theoretic approach that uses mean-squared error to choose nonnegative weights while accounting for outcome quality. I revisit a study on social distancing.
item.dc:creator: Chun Pong Lau

item.title: Sensitivity Analysis in Population Shares
item.description: arXiv:2611.05584v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Empirical work often relies on assumptions on the distribution of random variables, such as potential outcomes or latent variables, to identify some parameter of interest. We introduce a unified framework for assessing the sensitivity of a target estimand to relaxing these distributional assumptions for a given share of the population. We derive bounds on the values the estimand can take as this share varies between 0 and 1, and compute the bounds using tractable finite-dimensional programs. We propose plug-in estimators for the bounds and characterize their large sample properties. We also show that our bounds recover exact nonparametric sharp bounds at no additional computational cost, and introduce summary measures that separate misspecification uncertainty from sampling uncertainty and rank studies by their robustness. We apply our framework to assess the robustness of (i) average treatment effects in randomized experiments with attrition, (ii) counterfactual predictions in structural models, and (iii) formula instruments. We provide R and Python packages implementing all our methods.
item.dc:creator: Filippo Palomba

item.title: Debiased Conditional Independence Tests for Causal Effects
item.description: arXiv:2611.05608v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose robust tests for causal effects on potentially high-dimensional outcomes where there may be selection into treatment. These tests measure conditional independence of outcomes from treatment assignment by asking whether treatment can be predicted from outcomes more accurately than from covariates alone. We design three such tests of conditional independence. First, we propose a conditional randomization test based on an inverse propensity weighted mean squared error test statistic. If the propensity score is known, the test controls size in finite samples. Second, we propose a double-residualization approach, where we partial out covariate effects from both treatment and outcome-based treatment predictions, and test whether the correlation between the residuals is zero. Third, we propose a test based on an augmented inverse propensity weighted estimator built around doubly robust, Neyman-orthogonal population moments that are necessary and sufficient for conditional independence. Simulations show that all three tests improve power over a joint Wald test based on a seemingly unrelated regression across many non-linear settings, particularly under heavy tails, outliers, mixtures, heterogeneous effects, and effects with opposite signs.
item.dc:creator: Susan Athey, Maria Nareklishvili, Jann Spiess

item.title: On the Theory of Multidimensional Stationary Random Processes (1941): Translation and Commentary
item.description: arXiv:2611.05644v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This edition provides an English translation and commentary on V. N. Zasukhin's 1941 note "On the Theory of Multidimensional Stationary Random Processes," originally published in Doklady Akademii Nauk SSSR, 33(7-8), 435-437. The note states a multivariate extension of Wold's decomposition: an orthogonal decomposition into singular and regular components, a one-sided moving-average representation of the regular component in terms of orthonormal innovation sequences, and a spectral criterion for regularity of full rank. The latter combines absolute continuity of the spectral functions with positivity and logarithmic integrability of the determinant of the spectral density matrix. Whittle (1953) explicitly credited Zasukhin with the multivariate generalization. The original results are presented without detailed proofs. A separate editorial note discusses their historical reception and explains the terminology. A retypeset Russian transcription is included for comparison.
item.dc:creator: Bulat Gafarov, Madina Karamysheva

item.title: Neural Score-Driven Volatility and Risk Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2611.05778v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a score-driven volatility model in which no particular parametric innovation distribution needs to be specified. The proposed method relies on a lightweight neural network to represent the negative score of the innovation density. By integrating and normalizing the learned score and imposing location-scale identification, we recover a flexible innovation density that can accommodate asymmetry, including negative skewness commonly observed in financial returns. Two estimation procedures are considered. A two-step procedure estimates the neural score by score matching and subsequently fits the volatility recursion with the identified density held fixed. A one-step procedure jointly refines the neural and volatility parameters under the conditional likelihood. We illustrate the practical relevance of the proposed method using eight international equity indices, with a separate evaluation of the high-volatility first half of 2020. The results show that the neural score-driven models are competitive with Gaussian and Student-$t$ GAS benchmarks that require a prespecified parametric innovation distribution, with particularly strong performance during the COVID-19 period.
item.dc:creator: Qianli Zhao, Chao Wang, Minh-Ngoc Tran, Richard Gerlach

item.title: Online Bayesian Inference for a Dirichlet Process Mixture of Binary Logit Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.06266v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Flexible travel behaviour models for preference heterogeneity have largely remained within the batch-estimation paradigm. The growing availability of continuously collected behavioural data, for example from smartphone applications, highlights the need for methods that update posterior inference on such heterogeneity as new observations arrive. This study proposes an online Bayesian inference method for a Dirichlet process mixture of binary logit models. The main challenge is to update the posterior as observations arrive while allowing the latent cluster structure to expand and historical cluster assignments to be revised. We develop a sequential Monte Carlo sampler using a sequence of P\'olya--Gamma-augmented partial-data posteriors, local particle-weight corrections, and recursively maintained sufficient statistics. Each observation's contribution can be added, removed, or replaced in these summaries, supporting both sequential coefficient updating and rejuvenation that revisits historical cluster assignments. The simulation study shows that observation-by-observation sequential updating yields final posterior summaries close to those obtained by batch Markov chain Monte Carlo. Sensitivity analyses further demonstrate trade-offs between posterior approximation accuracy and computational cost as the number of particles and rejuvenation settings are varied. An illustrative empirical application shows how the method tracks posterior evolution and produces observation-specific provisional posterior summaries with low latency as real-world trip records are processed sequentially. The proposed approach provides a methodological foundation for online inference in travel behaviour models with parameter heterogeneity and for future extensions to richer choice structures, low-latency decision support, and online anomaly screening.
item.dc:creator: Hajime Watanabe, Charisma F. Choudhury, Stephane Hess

item.title: Approximate minimax regret for conditionally similar tests
item.description: arXiv:2611.06557v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct approximately minimax regret optimal tests in a scalar Gaussian instrumental variables experiment. This example shows how conditionally similar tests allow a novel approximation approach, allowing us to optimize weights over alternatives to minimize worst-case power regret. Stochastic mirror descent and averaging yield finite-iteration guarantees with exact conditional similarity. We establish bounds for exact and simulated powers and illustrate the procedure numerically. This initial algorithm shows how existing nearly-optimal test computation methods can be extended to include composite alternative hypothesis sets without the computational cost associated with maintaining size control.
item.dc:creator: Andr\'es Aradillas Fern\'andez

item.title: Regression with Many Generated Controls
item.description: arXiv:2611.06855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider linear regression when some covariates are endogenous, a variable sufficient to control for endogeneity exists but is latent, and the practitioner can generate many proxies for the latent control. For instance, one could cheaply but imperfectly impute the latent control using different AI/ML methods, each generating a different proxy. There are several options the practitioner might consider in this scenario: including all proxies or factors computed from the proxies as controls, instrumental variables estimation, and some nonlinear variants thereof. We use a transparent model to derive the implicit estimand each approach targets, determine when these estimands recover the parameter of interest, and provide some practical recommendations. We show that with a sufficiently rich set of generated controls, practitioners can consistently estimate the parameter of interest without relying on validation data.
item.dc:creator: Timothy Christensen, Daniel Vebman

item.title: Offline Learning of Reserve Prices from Censored Bids
item.description: arXiv:2611.06067v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study how a seller can learn a reserve price for a second-price auction from censored historical bid data. Because values below past reserves are unobserved, even unlimited data may not reveal which reserve earns the most revenue. Under a monotone hazard rate (MHR) assumption, we characterize exactly when an optimal reserve is identified, even though the value distribution may not be: either revenue has not yet begun to fall at the lowest historical reserve, so the best reserve lies among the observed bids, or the censored fraction is as large as MHR allows, which pins down the entire distribution. When identification fails, we derive the reserve that minimizes worst-case revenue regret over distributions consistent with the data, and prove that this unique minimax reserve and its regret depend on just two observable quantities: the censored fraction and the hazard just above the lowest historical reserve. With $N$ historical bidders, the optimal reserve is learned with expected worst-case regret $O(N^{-1/2})$ when it lies among the observed bids, and $O(N^{-1})$ from the censored count alone when the censored fraction is as large as MHR allows and the optimum lies at or below the lowest reserve. In the nonidentifiable regime, plugging estimates of the two quantities into the minimax reserve gives expected worst-case regret within $O(N^{-2/5})$ of the population minimum under local density smoothness, with a matching minimax lower bound on a smooth class. Beyond MHR, we solve the minimax problem for regular and unrestricted distributions and prove an $O(N^{-2/5})$ learning bound in the regular nonidentifiable regime, given known bounds on the boundary parameters. Experiments on synthetic and eBay data show gains from exploiting MHR and the benefits of the robust rule when parametric models are misspecified.
item.dc:creator: Lavanya Marla, Yunzong Xu, Boxuan Zhou

item.title: The Linear Programming Approach to Partially Identified Models
item.description: arXiv:2503.14940v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In many partially identified models, sharp bounds on structural or causal parameters are values of linear programs (LPs) with estimated coefficients. We introduce a debiased penalty estimator of the LP value. It is pointwise root-n-consistent whenever the population feasible set is nonempty and bounded. Although no estimator is uniformly consistent over the unrestricted collection of distributions, ours retains a one-sided guarantee: the extent to which it can overestimate a sharp lower bound vanishes uniformly. Under a condition ruling out weak identification of the bound, it is also uniformly consistent. We develop two inference procedures exploiting LP structure: a simple pointwise procedure with exact asymptotic coverage, and a uniformly valid procedure. In simulations calibrated to Holmes (2011), our estimator avoids the anticonservative bias of unregularized benchmark estimators and the conservativeness of the set expansion estimator. Both inference procedures deliver reliable coverage, small excess length, and orders-of-magnitude computational gains over test-inversion benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Andrei Voronin

item.title: A Relaxation Approach to Synthetic Control
item.description: arXiv:2508.01793v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The synthetic control method (SCM) is widely used for constructing the counterfactual of a treated unit based on data from control units in a donor pool. Allowing the donor pool to contain more control units than time periods, we propose SCM-relaxation, an adaptation of the stable-balancing framework to the synthetic control setting. This approach minimizes an information-theoretic measure of the weights subject to a set of relaxed linear inequality constraints in addition to the simplex constraint. When the donor pool exhibits a group structure, SCM-relaxation approximates the equal weights within each group to diversify the prediction risk. Asymptotically, the proposed estimator achieves oracle performance in terms of out-of-sample prediction accuracy, and can be used to conduct inference about the average treatment effect on the treated. Our empirical application assesses the economic impact of Brexit on the United Kingdom's real GDP.
item.dc:creator: Chengwang Liao, Zhentao Shi, Yapeng Zheng

item.title: How Different are Different Differences-in-Differences? A Large-Scale Meta-Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.39995v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: I use AI-assisted replication to assess the empirical importance of negative weights in two-way fixed effects (TWFE) estimation, analyzing 1,430 staggered-adoption specifications from 116 economics papers. TWFE estimates are highly correlated with modern difference-in-differences estimates, with sign reversals in 12.0-14.9% of comparisons and greater precision for TWFE. Hierarchical models accounting for estimation noise imply estimand correlations of 91-97% and a 0.7-2.4% probability of a statistically significant TWFE estimate opposing the modern estimand's sign. These findings suggest negative weights may be a less serious problem in practice and illustrate how AI can support systematic, large-scale empirical assessments of new econometric methods.
item.dc:creator: Peter Hull

item.title: A Granular Framework for Construction Material Price Forecasting: Econometric and Machine-Learning Approaches
item.description: arXiv:2512.09360v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The persistent volatility of construction material prices poses significant risks to cost estimation, budgeting, and project delivery, underscoring the urgent need for granular and scalable forecasting methods. This study develops a forecasting framework that leverages the Construction Specifications Institute (CSI) MasterFormat as the target data structure, enabling predictions at the six-digit Section level and supporting detailed cost projections across a wide spectrum of building materials. To enhance predictive accuracy, the framework integrates explanatory variables such as raw material prices, commodity indexes, and macroeconomic indicators. Five time-series models, long short-term memory (LSTM), autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA), vector error correction model (VECM), vanilla Transformer, and Chronos-Bolt, were evaluated under both baseline configurations (using CSI data only) and extended versions with explanatory variables. Results demonstrate that incorporating explanatory variables significantly improves predictive performance across all models. Among the tested approaches, the LSTM model consistently achieved the highest accuracy, with root mean squared error (RMSE) values as low as 4.19 and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) values of 1.60 based on Division 06 as a representative demonstration, representing improvements of up to 59% over the traditional statistical time-series model, ARIMA. Validation across multiple CSI Divisions within the residential-material confirmed the framework's scalability, while Division 06 (Wood, Plastics, and Composites) is presented in detail as a demonstration case. This research offers a robust methodology that enables owners and contractors to improve budgeting practices and achieve more reliable cost estimation at the definitive level.
item.dc:creator: Boge Lyu, Qianye Yin, Iris Denise Tommelein, Hanyang Liu, Karnamohit Ranka, Karthik Yeluripati, Junzhe Shi

item.title: Valuation Reveals Uncertainty
item.description: arXiv:2606.29572v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper studies the recovery of uncertainty from dynamic sublinear valuation rules. Robust valuation assigns each payoff its worst-case expected value over a family of plausible models, thereby inducing a dynamic sublinear valuation rule. While valuation rules are observable in practice, the underlying uncertainty structure remains latent. Under suitable conditions, we show that an uncertainty structure can be recovered from an observed valuation rule and provide an explicit recovery procedure. The construction characterizes the joint uncertainty in the discount factor and the law of the state process.
item.dc:creator: Jongjin Park, David Criens, Hyungbin Park

item.title: Curvature-Calibrated Quasi-Bayesian Updating for Moment-Restricted Models
item.description: arXiv:2608.19634v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quadratic moment-based quasi-posteriors depend on a weighting matrix governing both the contributions of moment conditions and the scale of posterior uncertainty. We propose curvature-calibrated quasi-Bayesian (CCQB) updating, which iteratively evaluates the inverse of the estimated moment covariance (or long-run covariance) at the center of the resulting fixed-weight quasi-posterior. A two-part stopping rule monitors changes in the center and Monte Carlo error in estimating it. Under local regularity conditions, the ideal calibration map is contractive, and its fixed point is root-N consistent. The calibrated quasi-posterior and the sampling distribution of its center have the inverse Godambe information matrix as their root-N-scale covariance. Simulations show substantial gains over identity weighting. Further iteration has little effect in linear designs but improves calibration for some parameters in nonlinear settings, although nominal coverage is not uniformly achieved. An application to longitudinal childhood wheeze data illustrates the method under within-subject dependence.
item.dc:creator: Masahiro Tanaka
